title: Where do you live?
goal: Say where you're from and where you live, use the place ending -n, give your age and job, and count to a hundred.
bekal: answer *nongoa zara?* and *non bizi zara?* in full
attach the place ending *-n/-an* to city names and ordinary nouns
count to a hundred the Basque way, in twenties

dialogs.title: Elkarrizketa — Euskaltegiko lehen klasea
dialogs.intro: The first class at the euskaltegi. Ainhoa goes around asking her new students about themselves.

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.text: Egun on denoi! Nor zara zu?
lines.id: Good morning, everyone! Who are you?
lines.literal: day good all-to! who are you?

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.id: And where do you live now?

lines.speaker: Marie:
lines.text: Orain Bilbon bizi naiz, ikasle etxe batean.
lines.id: Now I live in Bilbo, in a student residence.
lines.literal: now Bilbo-in living am, student house one-in.

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.id: And you, Budi? Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Indonesiakoa naiz, Jakartakoa. Baina orain Bilbon bizi naiz.
lines.id: I'm from Indonesia, from Jakarta. But now I live in Bilbo.
lines.literal: Indonesia-from-one am, Jakarta-from-one. but now Bilbo-in living am.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hogeita bost urte ditut. Eta zu, Marie?
lines.literal: twenty-and five year I-have-them. and you, Marie?

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.text: Ez zara zaharra! Eta zu, Iker? Non bizi zara?
lines.id: You're not old! And you, Iker? Where do you live?
lines.literal: not are old-the! and you, Iker? where living are?

lines.speaker: Iker:
lines.text: Donostian bizi naiz, baina Bilbon lan egiten dut.
lines.id: I live in Donostia, but I work in Bilbo.
lines.literal: Donostia-in living am, but Bilbo-in work doing I-have-it.

lines.speaker: Ainhoa:
lines.text: Ondo. Ongi etorri denoi, eta has gaitezen!
lines.id: Good. Welcome, everyone, and let's begin!
lines.literal: good. well come all-to, and begin let-us.

notes: **Bizi naiz — two words, one meaning.** *Bizi izan* means "to live". The *bizi* part never changes; only the *izan* after it does: *bizi naiz*, *bizi zara*, *bizi da*, *bizi gara*. You'll meet this "fixed word + auxiliary" pattern again and again — *lan egin*, *hitz egin*, *lo egin*.

**Nongoa and non ask two different things.** *Nongoa zara?* asks about **origin** ("where are you from?"), *Non bizi zara?* about **where you live now**. Budi answers them differently: he's from Jakarta, he lives in Bilbo. Keep the two questions apart.

**Zenbat urte dituzu? — you "have" your age.** Literally "how many years do you have?" — just like Spanish and French. The answer is *… urte ditut*. *Ditut/dituzu* is the auxiliary for **plural** things; it's unpacked fully in Unit 5. For now, memorize these two sentences as they are.

**Baina, eta, edo — the three most common linking words.** *Eta* (and), *baina* (but), *edo* (or). All three stand between the two parts of a sentence, exactly as in English. This is one corner of Basque with no surprises at all.

blocks.text: Basque has no word for "in" or "at". It glues *-n* onto the end of the place word instead. The exact form depends on the word's last letter.

blocks.text: Notice that ordinary nouns take *-an*, which is really the article *-a* plus *-n*: *etxe + a + n* → *etxean*, "house-the-in". A word that already ends in *-a* just adds *-n*: *gela* → *gelan*.

blocks.title: Basque cities have two faces
items: Many cities have a Basque name and a Spanish name that are very different: **Bilbo** = Bilbao, **Donostia** = San Sebastián, **Gasteiz** = Vitoria, **Iruñea** = Pamplona, **Baiona** = Bayonne.
Inside a Basque sentence, use the Basque name. Dropping "San Sebastián" into the middle of a euskara sentence sounds like mixing two languages in one breath.
*Euskal Herria* is the name of the whole region — literally "the land of euskara". It's not a country but a cultural region covering seven provinces in two countries.

sections.title: Numbers from twenty to a hundred

blocks.text: Here Basque shows off its distinctive way of counting: the basic unit isn't ten but **twenty**. Forty is "two times twenty", sixty "three times twenty", eighty "four times twenty".

There's really only one pattern: take the nearest multiple of twenty below, add *-ta*, then the rest. *Berrogeita hamazazpi* = 40 + 17 = 57. It sounds long, and it is — even native speakers often use Spanish numbers for prices in shops. But for ages, dates, and small amounts, the Basque forms are used every day.

blocks.title: Age: years are something you have
items: *Zenbat urte dituzu?* — "How old are you?" (literally: how many years do you have?)
*Nire aitak berrogeita hamar urte ditu.* — "My father is 50."
Notice that *urte* stays bare, without *-a*: after a number, a noun never takes the article.

blocks.text: Notice the *n*- family: *nor*, *non*, *nora*, *nondik*, *noiz*, *nola*, *nongo* — they all start with the same sound, much like the English wh- words. Learning them as one group is far easier than one by one.

blocks.title: The word-order rule that matters
items: The question word must stand **right before the verb**. *Non **bizi zara**?* is right; ***Non zara bizi?*** is wrong.
The same rule applies to answers: whatever matters most goes right before the verb. *Bilbon bizi naiz* answers "where"; *ni bizi naiz Bilbon* sounds like a sentence whose words got scattered.
For yes/no questions, just raise your voice at the end — or slip *al* in before the verb: *Euskalduna **al** zara?* ("Are you Basque?"). *Al* is polite and very typically Basque.
